quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Community fridges, placed outside shops and libraries, let anyone leave surplus food or take what they need. Volunteers check them daily and clean them weekly. Organizers say the idea works because it removes the stigma of asking for help: no forms, no questions. Some fridges are emptied within hours of being stocked. Critics note that fridges cannot replace wider support, but supporters reply that they meet a need while larger solutions are debated.
options: How Community Fridges Share Surplus Food
Why Some People Avoid Asking for Help
quests.correctAnswer: How Community Fridges Share Surplus Food
quests.hint: Ask what the passage describes at its center, before the critics and supporters appear.
quests.explanation: Cleaning, the debate, and the stigma are parts of the picture. The passage explains what the fridges are and why they work.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice covers how the fridges operate, why people use them, and the response to them.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Start planning at least three weeks before the exam. List every topic, then rate each as strong, medium, or weak. Give the weak topics the most time early on, and save the last week for practice tests instead of new material. Include rest days: students who study every day without breaks often remember less. Adjust the plan weekly rather than abandoning it when you fall behind.
options: Why Students Remember Less Without Breaks
Rating Topics as Strong, Medium, or Weak
Building a Realistic Exam Study Plan
quests.correctAnswer: Building a Realistic Exam Study Plan
quests.hint: Count how many separate pieces of advice there are, and what they aim to produce.
quests.explanation: Rating topics, practice tests, and rest days are individual pieces of advice. The passage puts them together into a plan.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title combines the timeline, priorities, rest, and adjustment into one workable plan.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: On a video call, small habits matter more than expected. Muting your microphone when you are not speaking cuts background noise for everyone. Looking at the camera, rather than the screen, gives others a sense of eye contact; if the connection freezes, switching off your video often restores the audio. Finally, tell participants in advance if you must leave early, so the meeting does not stall waiting for you.
options: Simple Etiquette for Better Video Calls
Choosing a Quiet Room for Meetings
quests.correctAnswer: Simple Etiquette for Better Video Calls
quests.hint: Notice that most tips are about how to behave, not just about fixing technology.
quests.explanation: The frozen connection is one technical tip. Room choice and dislike of meetings are not mentioned.
quests.whyThisTitle: Muting, eye contact, and giving notice are all courtesies that improve calls.

quests.correctAnswer: Free English Classes for Adults

quests.explanation: Childcare, levels, and bringing a friend are all facts about the course. The announcement's headline is the free class for adults.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When comparing packaged foods, start with the serving size, since all the numbers refer to it. A package that looks like one portion may contain two or three servings. Next, check sugar and salt, which are often higher than expected in sauces and breakfast cereals. Finally, read the ingredient list: ingredients appear in order of weight, so the first few are the main components.
options: Reading a Food Label with Confidence
A Guide to Choosing Healthy Sauces from the Supermarket
quests.correctAnswer: Reading a Food Label with Confidence
quests.hint: The passage says 'start,' 'next,' and 'finally.' What is being done in that order?
quests.explanation: Sugar in cereals and the ingredient order are parts of the reading. The passage teaches a way to read the whole label.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title covers serving size, sugar and salt, and ingredients as steps in reading a label.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: For a first bike commute, ride the route on a weekend to check for hills, busy junctions, and places to lock your bike. Wear something bright and carry a spare tube and a small pump. Leave ten minutes earlier than needed the first week, since everything takes longer while you learn. If you arrive sweaty, a change of shirt in your bag solves most problems.
options: Riding the Route on a Weekend
Avoiding Sweat on the Way to Work
Preparing for Your First Bike Commute
quests.correctAnswer: Preparing for Your First Bike Commute
quests.hint: Ask what all these separate tips prepare the reader for.
quests.explanation: The weekend ride, spare tube, and shirt change are individual tips. The text is a set of preparations for a first commute.
quests.whyThisTitle: Route checks, equipment, timing, and clothing all prepare a newcomer for commuting by bike.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In a small canal town, visitors now outnumber residents ten to one on summer weekends. Shopkeepers welcome the income, but residents say that sidewalks are blocked and rents have risen as homes turn into holiday rentals. The council has introduced a small entry fee for day visitors and limits on new rental licenses. It is still too early to say whether the measures will work.
quests.correctAnswer: A Town Crowded by Visitors
quests.hint: The passage presents a problem, different views, and a response. What connects them?
quests.explanation: Fees, rents, and shopkeeper income are all pieces of the situation. The passage covers the tension caused by so many visitors.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice covers the crowding and the mixed reactions and actions that follow from it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A good cover letter is short and specific. Begin by naming the job and saying, in one sentence, why you want it. In the middle, choose two examples from your experience that match what the advertisement asks for, and explain what you achieved rather than only what you did. Close by thanking the reader and stating that you would welcome an interview. One page is enough.
options: Thanking the Reader at the Close
A Guide to Choosing Examples from Your Experience
quests.correctAnswer: Writing a Focused Cover Letter
quests.hint: Consider the beginning, middle, and end the passage describes.
quests.explanation: Examples and the closing are two of the sections. The passage's subject is the letter as a whole.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the advice on the opening, examples, and closing that make a letter focused.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Free Wi-Fi in cafés and airports is convenient, but anyone on the same network may be able to see unprotected data. Avoid logging into banking or shopping accounts on these networks; if you must, use a virtual private network or your phone's mobile data instead. Turn off automatic connection so your device does not join unknown networks, and check that websites begin with 'https' before entering a password.
quests.correctAnswer: Staying Safe on Public Wi-Fi
quests.hint: The passage begins with convenience and moves to risk. What does the advice protect?
quests.explanation: A virtual network and 'https' checks are specific measures. Finding Wi-Fi is the reverse of the passage's concern.
quests.whyThisTitle: The warnings and precautions all aim to protect users on shared networks.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Renting a car abroad is usually straightforward, but a few checks save trouble. Confirm that your driving license is accepted, or whether you need an international permit. Photograph the car from every side before you leave the lot, so that existing scratches are on record. Check whether the tank should be returned full, since refueling charges can be high. Finally, read the insurance terms to understand what you would pay if something went wrong.
options: Checks to Make Before Renting a Car Abroad
quests.correctAnswer: Checks to Make Before Renting a Car Abroad
quests.hint: How many separate checks are listed, and when should they be done?
quests.explanation: Photographs, insurance, and licenses are each one check. The passage gathers them all as things to do before setting off.
quests.whyThisTitle: The license, photographs, fuel, and insurance checks all belong to preparing for a rental.

A Manager Thanks the Team After an Open Day

quests.passage: In many group projects, one or two members end up doing most of the work. Teachers suggest simple ways to prevent this: assign each person a specific part at the first meeting, agree on deadlines that come before the real one, and check progress in a short weekly call. When roles are clear, it is easier to notice problems early and to speak about them politely.
options: Preventing Unequal Work in Group Projects
Agreeing on Deadlines That Come Before the Real One
quests.correctAnswer: Preventing Unequal Work in Group Projects
quests.hint: Ask what problem is described and what the teachers' suggestions are for.
quests.explanation: The deadlines and check-ins are two suggestions. The passage centers on a problem and methods to avoid it.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title combines the imbalance the passage starts with and the practices that prevent it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Financial advisers often recommend keeping a small emergency fund, enough to cover a few months of essential costs. The money is not meant for holidays or new gadgets; its purpose is to absorb surprises like a broken washing machine or a sudden loss of work. Building it does not have to be dramatic. Setting aside a small fixed amount each payday, in a separate account, is often enough to make progress.
options: Paying for a Broken Washing Machine
The Purpose of a Small Emergency Fund
quests.correctAnswer: The Purpose of a Small Emergency Fund
quests.hint: Notice the difference between what the fund is for and what it is not for.
quests.explanation: Regular saving and the washing machine are details. The passage explains the purpose of the fund and how to begin one.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects the purpose of the fund and the modest way to start it.

quests.passage: On Friday evenings in July, the town park will show free films on a large outdoor screen. Doors open at seven for picnics, and the film begins at sunset. Chairs and blankets are welcome, but please leave large umbrellas at home. Food stalls will sell drinks and snacks, with all profits going to the local youth club. In case of rain, films will be moved to the community hall.
options: Free Outdoor Film Nights in the Park
Food Stalls Supporting the Youth Club
quests.correctAnswer: Free Outdoor Film Nights in the Park
quests.hint: What event is being promoted, and what are the extra details?
quests.explanation: The stalls, the chairs, and the rain plan are all extra information. The announcement promotes the film nights.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the event that every practical detail relates to.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Most people have thousands of photos on their phone and no copy anywhere else. If the phone is lost or breaks, the pictures disappear with it. A simple habit protects them: turn on automatic backup to a cloud account, and every few months copy the most important pictures to a separate drive. The cloud handles daily accidents, while the drive protects against a forgotten password or a closed account.
options: Two Simple Ways to Protect Your Photos
How to Choose a Cloud Account
Losing a Phone with Thousands of Pictures
quests.correctAnswer: Two Simple Ways to Protect Your Photos
quests.hint: The passage opens with a risk. What is offered as protection?
quests.explanation: The loss of a phone and forgotten passwords are risks. The passage's main point is how two kinds of backup protect against them.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the two backups and the different risks each covers.

quests.passage: If you notice a problem in your neighborhood, such as a broken streetlight or a pothole, you can report it online or by phone. Give the exact location, describe the problem in a sentence or two, and add a photo if you can. You will receive a reference number, which you should keep to follow up. Most simple repairs are scheduled within ten working days.
options: Reporting a Neighborhood Problem to the Council
quests.correctAnswer: Reporting a Neighborhood Problem to the Council
quests.hint: Think about what a resident wants to do and what the text explains.
quests.explanation: Photos, repair timing, and the reference number are single details. The text explains the whole process of making a report.
quests.whyThisTitle: It covers how to report, what to include, and what to expect afterward.

quests.passage: A helpful online review describes what happened rather than only how the writer felt. Mention what you ordered or used, the date, and the outcome, so other readers can judge if their experience would be similar. Be fair: if the food was good but the service slow, say both. Avoid personal attacks on staff; businesses often respond to specific, calm comments, and readers trust them more.
quests.correctAnswer: Writing Useful Online Reviews
quests.hint: Look for what all the advice has in common.
quests.explanation: Fairness, specifics, and business responses are each part of what makes a review helpful. The whole text is about writing helpful reviews.
quests.whyThisTitle: Details, fairness, and calm wording all make a review more useful to others.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: After hours at a screen, many people notice tired or dry eyes. Eye specialists suggest a simple pause: every twenty minutes, look at something about six meters away for twenty seconds. Blinking more often also helps, as does keeping the screen slightly below eye level. If discomfort continues despite these changes, it is worth having your eyes checked.
options: Easing Eye Strain from Screen Use
quests.correctAnswer: Easing Eye Strain from Screen Use
quests.hint: Ask what the problem is and what set of remedies the passage gives.
quests.explanation: Blinking, looking away, and getting a check are three pieces of advice. The passage puts them together as ways to reduce discomfort.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice combines the problem with the several habits that help.

quests.passage: Timetables can look like grids of numbers, but they are easy to read once you know the pattern. Each column is a train and each row a station. Find your starting station in the left column, follow the row across to the time you want, then read down the column to see when the same train reaches your destination. Symbols beside times often show that a train runs only on certain days.
options: How to Choose the Fastest Train Home
How to Read a Train Timetable
quests.correctAnswer: How to Read a Train Timetable
quests.hint: Think about the reader's skill: what will they be able to do afterward?
quests.explanation: Symbols and finding a station are steps within the explanation. Choosing the fastest train is never discussed.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the layout and the steps for finding a train's times.

Rooms with screens are reserved for groups of three or more.
options: How to Book a Library Study Room
Losing a Room After Fifteen Minutes
quests.correctAnswer: How to Book a Library Study Room

quests.explanation: The screens rule and the fifteen-minute rule are conditions. The passage explains the booking process and how it works.

options: Getting the Most from a Doctor's Appointment
quests.correctAnswer: Getting the Most from a Doctor's Appointment
quests.hint: Ask what all the tips help the patient to achieve.
quests.explanation: Symptoms, medicines, and asking for repetition are each one tip. The passage's goal is a more useful appointment.

quests.passage: When a city organized a car-free week, nearly a thousand households signed up to try other ways of getting around. Most discovered that trips under three kilometers were quicker by bike or on foot than expected; some found that a bus route they had never used suited them well. About a third said they would drive less in future, while others returned to their cars but with a new sense of the alternatives.
options: Cycling Short Trips Across the City
quests.correctAnswer: Lessons from a Car-Free Week
quests.hint: What do the different results of the experiment have in common?
quests.explanation: Cycling, buses, and returning to cars are individual outcomes. The passage reports what households learned overall.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title covers the varied discoveries, and the mixed changes in habits that resulted.

Returning a Permission Slip by Friday

They suggest joining one club rather than five, attending the introductory sessions offered by the library and student services, and keeping a regular sleep routine. Feeling homesick is common, and most students say it fades.
quests.correctAnswer: Settling In at University
quests.hint: Consider the reassurance and the advice together.
quests.explanation: Clubs, homesickness, and library sessions are details. The passage gives realistic expectations and practical advice for new students.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many households throw away food that is still safe because the date on the package is misunderstood. A 'use by' date is about safety and should be respected, especially for meat, fish, and dairy. A 'best before' date, by contrast, concerns quality: after it passes, the food may lose flavor or texture but is usually safe to eat. Learning the difference can reduce waste and save money.
options: Throwing Away Safe Food Each Week
Checking Meat and Fish Before Cooking
quests.correctAnswer: Understanding Food Date Labels
quests.hint: What is the passage contrasting, and why does it matter?
quests.explanation: Waste, meat and fish, and savings are effects or examples. The passage explains the two kinds of label and how they differ.
quests.whyThisTitle: It focuses on the difference between the two labels, which the rest of the passage supports.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When reading a chart in a report, begin with the title and the labels on each axis, since they tell you what is being measured. Then look at the scale: bars that start above zero can make small differences look large; only after that should you compare the shapes and heights. Finally, read the note under the chart, where the source and any limits of the data are usually given.
options: Reading a Chart Carefully Before Drawing Conclusions
Looking at Sources Under a Chart
quests.correctAnswer: Reading a Chart Carefully Before Drawing Conclusions
quests.hint: The passage says 'only after that.' What does that phrase suggest about the order?
quests.explanation: The scale, the source note, and the comparison are all steps. The passage argues for a careful order of reading before judging.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title captures the sequence of checks that comes before forming conclusions.
